title: Ancient Greece · Episode 1
chapters: Athens and Sparta: the Greek city-states

units.t: Ancient Greece. Episode one.
In this episode: Athens and Sparta: the Greek city-states, The original Olympic Games, The birth of democracy and Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis.
Part one. Athens and Sparta: the Greek city-states.
Ancient Greece was never one country.
It was hundreds of fiercely independent cities, and two of them couldn't have been more different.
A land of city-states.
Greece's mountains and islands split people into small communities.
From around 800 BC, these grew into city-states, each called a polis, the root of words like politics and police.
A polis was a city plus its farmland, with its own government, laws, army, coins and gods.
Scholars have counted roughly a thousand, most with only a few thousand people.
Greeks shared a language, religion, the oracle at Delphi and the Olympic Games, and called non-Greek speakers 'barbarians'.
Yet they fought each other constantly.
Farmland was scarce, so from the 700s BC cities sent settlers to found independent colonies.
Marseille began as Massalia, Naples as Neapolis and Istanbul as Byzantium.
Athens: the city of ideas.
Athens, built around the rocky hill of the Acropolis, grew rich from trade, the silver mines at Laurion and its powerful navy.
In the 400s BC it became the cultural capital of the Greek world.
Athenian citizens governed themselves in an early democracy, debating in the Assembly and trading in the agora, the bustling marketplace and meeting ground.
The city produced philosophers like Socrates and Plato, playwrights like Sophocles, and the historian Thucydides.
Its most famous building, the Parthenon, a marble temple to the goddess Athena, was completed in 432 BC and still stands above the modern city.
Sparta: the city of soldiers.
Sparta, in the southern Peloponnese, took a very different path.
At about age seven, boys left home for the agoge, a harsh state-run training system that taught endurance, discipline and fighting.
Adult men lived and ate in army messes and were banned from trade, so their full-time job was war.
Spartan women had unusual freedom: they exercised outdoors, owned land and ran estates.
All this rested on the helots, a huge enslaved population who did the farming and outnumbered Spartan citizens many times over.
Fear of a helot revolt shaped Spartan life.
Laconic and balanced.
Spartans were famous for saying a lot in few words.
According to ancient writers, when Philip II of Macedon threatened, 'If I invade Laconia, I will destroy you', they replied with one word: 'If.'
That's where laconic comes from.
Most of what we know comes from outsiders, so some is myth.
Sparta's government was unusual too.
Two kings from two royal families led the army and performed religious duties.
A council of elders, the gerousia, had 28 men over 60 plus the kings, and prepared laws.
Five ephors, elected every year, could supervise and even put the kings on trial.
An assembly of adult Spartan men approved major decisions by shouting.
Greeks admired this balance.
The Peloponnesian War.
As Athens built an empire of allied cities, Sparta and its allies grew alarmed.
War broke out in 431 BC and lasted, on and off, 27 years.
Athens had the stronger navy, Sparta the stronger army.
A plague in 430 BC killed perhaps a quarter of Athens' population, and a disastrous invasion of Sicily cost thousands of lives.
With Persian money, Sparta built a fleet, and in 404 BC a starving Athens surrendered.
The city-states kept fighting, and Thebes broke Sparta's army at Leuctra in 371 BC, freeing many helots.
Philip II of Macedon then defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC.
The age of independent city-states was over, but their ideas about citizenship, law and debate have lasted thousands of years.
The key idea: Greece was never one country but many independent cities, each called a polis, linked by shared culture.
Part two. The original Olympic Games.
For more than a thousand years, Greeks gathered at Olympia to run, wrestle and race chariots in honour of Zeus.
The ancient Games were holier, rougher and stranger than the modern version.
A festival and a truce.
Tradition dates the first Olympics to 776 BC, held every four years at Olympia in honour of Zeus.
The four-year gap, an Olympiad, became how Greeks counted years.
The sanctuary held temples and treasuries and a huge gold and ivory statue of Zeus by Phidias, later counted among the Seven Wonders.
On the middle day, priests sacrificed a hundred oxen and the meat fed the crowds.
Greece was hundreds of city-states, often at war.
Messengers announced a sacred truce, the ekecheiria, so athletes, trainers and spectators could travel safely and armies stayed out of Elis, which ran Olympia.
It did not stop wars and was sometimes broken: Sparta was banned and fined in 420 BC.
The modern Olympic Truce echoes the idea.
Running the stadion.
Tradition says the earliest Olympics had just one event: the stadion, a footrace of one length of the track, roughly 190 metres.
The winner gave his name to that Olympiad, so being the fastest man in Greece brought fame for generations.
Our word 'stadium' comes from this race.
Over time came longer foot races, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon, chariot and horse racing, and a race run in armour.
The pentathlon combined running, wrestling, discus, javelin and long jump, and long jumpers swung stone or metal weights called halteres to carry themselves further.
You can still walk through the stone tunnel into the ancient stadium at Olympia and stand on the starting line.
Naked, oiled and fierce.
Male athletes competed naked, their bodies rubbed with olive oil.
The Greeks admired the trained male body, and nudity in sport was part of their culture.
The combat events were tough.
Boxers wrapped their hands in leather straps rather than padded gloves, and bouts continued until one man gave up or could not go on.
The most dangerous event was the pankration, a mix of boxing and wrestling with very few rules.
Biting and eye-gouging were banned, but almost everything else was allowed, including strangleholds and bending fingers.
Fighters sometimes died.
Champions such as the wrestler Milo of Croton, said to have won at six Olympics, became legends whose stories were retold for centuries.
Women and the Games.
According to the ancient writer Pausanias, married women were not allowed to watch the Games, although unmarried girls may have been.
Women could not compete in the main events.
Yet there was a loophole.
In chariot racing, victory went to the horses' owner, not the driver.
The Spartan princess Kyniska bred and trained horses, and her team won the four-horse chariot race, probably in 396 BC and again in 392 BC.
She became the first woman named an Olympic victor, and a statue of her stood at Olympia.
Separately, a festival called the Heraia, in honour of the goddess Hera, included footraces for unmarried young women at Olympia itself.
Wreaths, rewards and the end.
An Olympic winner received a crown of wild olive leaves from a sacred tree near the temple of Zeus.
There were no silver or bronze medals; only winning counted.
Victors returned home as heroes, with cash, free meals for life and statues, and poets such as Pindar wrote victory odes.
Athletes caught bribing opponents were fined, and the money paid for bronze statues of Zeus, called Zanes, lining the path into the stadium, their bases naming the offenders.
Nero entered a chariot race in AD 67, fell from his chariot and was still declared winner.
As Christianity became official, pagan festivals were suppressed, and the Games ended in the late 300s or 400s, though the date is debated.
The first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896.
The key idea: The ancient Olympics were a religious festival for Zeus, protected by a sacred truce that let people travel safely.
Part three. The birth of democracy.
Around 2,500 years ago, the citizens of Athens tried something radical: letting ordinary people make the decisions.
Rule by the people.
Demokratia combines demos, the people, and kratos, power or rule.
Before democracy, Athens was ruled by aristocrats and, at times, by tyrants: strongmen who seized power.
Around 594 BC the lawmaker Solon eased debt slavery and gave poorer citizens a voice.

Then in 508 BC the reformer Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian society into ten new tribes that mixed people from the city, coast and countryside, so power flowed from citizens across the whole region rather than a few noble families.
This is usually counted as the birth of Athenian democracy, though it kept developing over the following decades.
Assembly and lottery.
Athens had a direct democracy: citizens didn't elect representatives, they decided themselves.
The Assembly met about 40 times a year on the Pnyx hillside.
Any citizen could attend, speak and vote, usually by show of hands, on war and peace, laws, taxes and treaties.
Imagine Australians gathering in person to vote on every new law.
Athenians thought elections favoured the rich, famous and persuasive, so most public jobs were filled by lot.
A council of 500 citizens, 50 from each tribe, was chosen randomly each year to prepare business for the Assembly.
Most people could serve only twice in a lifetime.
Only jobs needing expertise, like the ten military generals, were elected.
Courts without lawyers.
Athens had no police force, public prosecutors or professional judges.
Ordinary citizens brought cases themselves, and each side spoke in person, although they could pay a speechwriter.
Speeches were timed with a water clock, the klepsydra.
Juries were enormous, often 201, 501 or more citizens aged over 30, chosen by lot on the day to make bribery hard.
They voted by secret ballot using bronze discs and gave no reasons.
Socrates was tried by a jury of about 500.
Modern juries echo the same idea of ordinary citizens judging cases.
Paid to take part.
Democracy only works if ordinary people can afford to show up.
A labourer who spent a day on a jury lost a day's wages.
So in the mid-400s BC, the statesman Pericles introduced pay for jurors, and around 400 BC Athens began paying citizens to attend the Assembly as well.
The amounts were modest, roughly enough to live on for a day.
Critics grumbled that it encouraged idle crowds, but it meant farmers, craftsmen and rowers could genuinely take part.
Paying politicians and public servants today follows the same logic: public office shouldn't be only for the wealthy.
But who counted as a citizen was another matter.
Limits and legacy.
'Rule by the people' really meant rule by a minority of free men.
Women couldn't vote or hold office.
Enslaved people had no political rights.
Foreign residents, called metics, couldn't vote even after generations, and from 451 BC citizenship required both parents to be Athenian.
Once a year, citizens could vote to banish someone who seemed too powerful, scratching a name on a pottery shard called an ostrakon.
If enough votes were cast, probably at least 6,000, the person named most often was exiled for ten years, without a trial.
That gave us the word ostracise.
Plato distrusted democracy, and a jury sentenced Socrates in 399 BC.
Yet when modern democracies emerged, their founders studied Athens, and juries, referendums and citizens' assemblies chosen by lot still echo it.
The key idea: Athenian democracy began with Cleisthenes' reforms in 508 BC, shifting power from noble families to citizens.
Part four. Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis.
In the 400s BC the mighty Persian Empire invaded Greece twice.
Three battles decided whether Greek civilisation would survive.
An empire and a revolt.
By 500 BC, the Achaemenid Persian Empire ruled millions of people across three continents, linked by royal roads and governed through provinces called satrapies.
Greek cities on the coast of Ionia, in modern Turkey, were under Persian control.
When they rebelled in 499 BC, Athens and Eretria sent ships to help, and rebels burned the provincial capital of Sardis.
King Darius I crushed the revolt and resolved to punish Athens.
The wars that followed pitted a vast, well-organised empire against a handful of quarrelsome Greek city-states, and the outcome shaped the history of Europe.
Hoplites and triremes.
A Greek hoplite was a citizen-soldier who bought his own armour: a bronze helmet, a large round shield and a long thrusting spear.
Hoplites fought shoulder to shoulder in a phalanx, each man's shield partly protecting his neighbour, so discipline mattered more than individual heroics.
At sea, the key weapon was the trireme, a sleek warship rowed by about 170 oarsmen on three levels, with a bronze ram at the bow for smashing enemy hulls.
Rowers were often poorer citizens, and their importance to the navy later strengthened their political voice in Athens.
Marathon, 490 BC.
In 490 BC a Persian fleet landed at Marathon, about 40 kilometres from Athens.
The Athenians, joined by the small city of Plataea, were outnumbered but charged across the plain and won a decisive victory.
Herodotus says about 6,400 Persians died against 192 Athenians, figures that may be inflated.
He also tells of a runner, Pheidippides, who ran roughly 240 kilometres to Sparta to ask for help before the battle.
The more famous story, of a messenger running from Marathon to Athens and dying after announcing victory, appears in later writers.
It inspired the marathon race at the 1896 Olympics.
Thermopylae, 480 BC.
Darius died before he could strike again, so his son Xerxes planned a far bigger invasion.
His engineers built bridges of boats across the Hellespont and dug a canal through the Athos peninsula.
In 480 BC a vast army and navy moved into Greece.
Many Greek cities submitted.
Others, led by Sparta and Athens, formed an alliance.
A Greek force of several thousand, including King Leonidas and 300 Spartans, blocked the narrow pass of Thermopylae.
For three days they held off the Persians, including the elite Immortals.
Then a local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass.
Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with a rearguard of Spartans and several hundred Thespians, who were killed.
It was a defeat, but it bought time.
Salamis, Plataea and legacy.
The Persians burned an evacuated Athens.
Themistocles had earlier persuaded the city to spend a silver strike on around 200 triremes.
Now he lured the bigger Persian fleet into the narrow straits near Salamis, reportedly with a false message that the Greeks were about to flee.
Crowded together, the Persian ships couldn't manoeuvre, and the Greek triremes rammed and sank many.
In 479 BC, the Greeks defeated Mardonius's army at Plataea, and the invasions were over.
Had Persia won, Athens' democracy and golden age might never have happened.
Herodotus, writing a generation later, is called the father of history.
But he included myths and rumours, so his numbers, such as Xerxes' army of millions, are almost certainly exaggerated.
The key idea: Persia's punishment of Athens for helping a revolt set up a clash between an empire and quarrelsome city-states.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was a polis?
Answer. An independent city-state with its own laws.
Question two. What was the purpose of the sacred truce?
Answer. To let athletes and spectators travel safely to Olympia.
Question three. Why is Cleisthenes' reform of 508 BC counted as the birth of Athenian democracy?
Answer. It shifted power from noble families to citizens.
Question four. Why did Darius I resolve to punish Athens?
Answer. Athens had helped the Ionian Greek revolt.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
